summary: Shows that at high data rates, the 16-bit IP identification field is too small to avoid frequently mixing up fragments, and TCP and UDP checksums may not catch the resulting corrupted data. It describes experiments demonstrating the problem and discusses operational implications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If you cut many puzzles into pieces and mix them fast, the numbering runs out and pieces from different puzzles get glued together by mistake.

questions: ipv4 fragmentation problems at high speed
why is the ip id field too small
how does ip id wrap cause data corruption
subtitle: Why the 16-bit IPv4 ID field lets fragments from different datagrams get glued together at high data rates.

tldr.problem: IPv4 fragments are matched up by a 16-bit identification field. At high data rates that field wraps around faster than the receiver's reassembly timeout, so fragments of different datagrams can be spliced together.
tldr.mechanism: The note explains how the wrap-around causes mis-association, shows that 16-bit TCP and UDP checksums let some of the resulting corrupt datagrams through, and backs this up with UDP experiments at 100 Mbps.
tldr.outcome: Applications that depend on IPv4 fragmentation at high speed, and tunnels that add fragmentation, should avoid it or add stronger integrity checks. This is an Informational note, not a standard.

today: RFC 4963 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a description of a problem and its operational implications, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IPv4 header was designed when data rates were several orders of magnitude lower than today. This note describes a scale-related failure in the IP identification (ID) field: fragments may be assembled incorrectly often enough to undermine assumptions about how rarely data gets corrupted.

Fragmentation was already known to use the network inefficiently. This note describes a different problem, which can cause not only performance loss but also frequent data corruption. It is most relevant to UDP bulk transport tools that sometimes fragment every datagram, and to network equipment that ignores the Don't Fragment (DF) bit to work around MTU discovery problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers cut big messages into pieces and number them so they can be put back together. When messages are sent very fast, the numbers can repeat and the pieces get mixed up.

sections.title: Wrapping the IP ID Field
sections.content:
RFC 791 says the sender must choose an Identifier that is unique for a source, destination and protocol for as long as the datagram could be alive in the Internet. Strict conformance limits one direction between an address pair to no more than 65536 packets per protocol per maximum packet lifetime.

Many hosts ignore this, because it implies a very low maximum data rate. With 1500-byte packets and a 30-second lifetime, a host would exceed the limit at only about 26 Mbps. Filling a 1 Gbps interface would need 65536 packets in under a second. Some implementations also randomize the ID, which makes reuse happen probabilistically at any sending rate.

Receivers keep fragments in a reassembly buffer until the datagram is complete or the reassembly timeout expires (15 seconds is suggested in RFC 791). Fragments are matched by protocol number, ID value and the source and destination addresses. If the sender wraps the ID in less than that timeout, fragments of different datagrams can be mis-associated.

Mis-association can be self-propagating. If the first fragment of a datagram is lost and packets stay in order, the leftover fragments wait in the buffer. When the ID wraps, the next datagram's first fragment is joined to them, leaving that datagram incomplete too, and the cycle repeats every 65536 datagrams.

IPv6 is considerably less vulnerable because its fragment header has a 32-bit identification field, so the problem only appears at packet rates 65536 times higher.
sections.plainLanguage: The label on each message only has room for a certain number of different values. Send too many messages too quickly and labels get reused while old pieces are still waiting, so the wrong pieces get matched.

sections.title: Effects of Mis-Associated Fragments
sections.content:
When mis-associated fragments are delivered, the transport checksum should detect the bad datagram and discard it. Discards can still hurt performance, because loss-based congestion control reads them as non-congestive loss, which matters most when a large congestion window is needed.

The TCP and UDP checksum is only 16 bits long. If checksums are uniformly random, one mis-associated datagram in 65536 will pass. With a single mis-association cycle, corrupt data would reach the application once per 2^32 datagrams, and more often with several concurrent cycles.

Real data can be worse than random data. It is possible to build data sets where mis-associated fragments always have the same checksum, and some applications turn checksumming off for speed.
sections.plainLanguage: The quick check number on each message is small, so once in a while a wrongly glued message looks fine anyway and gets used.

sections.title: Experimental Observations
sections.content:
The authors used Reliable Blast UDP (RBUDP), a UDP bulk transfer tool from the QUANTA toolkit, chosen because it was easy to automate. Any UDP protocol with no extra corruption detection and configured to fragment would behave the same.

Files carried embedded sequence numbers and MD5 checksums in each fragment, so random corruption could be told apart from mis-association. A "constant" data set had constant UDP checksums and a "random" data set had uniformly random ones. Tests used 400 MB files sent in 1524-byte datagrams, so they were fragmented on Fast Ethernet with a 1500-byte MTU, at slightly less than 100 Mbps. A brief secondary flow induced loss in the primary flow.

Mis-association rates were typically a few hundredths of a percent. With the constant data set, every mis-associated fragment produced corruption. Sending approximately 10 TB of random data produced 8847668 UDP checksum errors and 121 corruptions of the data due to mis-associated fragments.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors sent huge files really fast and checked them afterwards. Many bad pieces were caught, but a small number of wrongly glued ones still slipped through.

sections.title: Preventing and Mitigating Mis-Association
sections.content:
The most straightforward fix is to avoid fragmentation with Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191, RFC 4821). That is not always feasible, and workarounds that clear or ignore the DF bit expose every IPv4 protocol to the problem.

Shortening the reassembly timeout could help, but the sender controls the rate and ID while the receiver controls the timeout. A timeout low enough for a fast sender would discard a slow sender's fragments, so it would need to be per peer, and NAT is likely to break per-peer tables. The note does not recommend a solution, though it believes a per-peer adaptive timeout would likely prevent mis-association where it is most common.

Tunnels that rely on fragmentation between their endpoints behave like end hosts with a single protocol type, so their aggregate rate can exceed 65536 per maximum packet lifetime. Even TCP traffic is affected. Operators should make sure the receiving end's reassembly timeout is short enough.

Where prevention is impractical, stronger integrity checking above IP mitigates the effects: IPsec AH discards corrupted datagrams, SCTP has a 32-bit checksum, and SSH message authentication codes prevent delivery of corrupted data. None of these removes the non-congestive loss. Applications sending at roughly 100 Mbps or higher, and devices such as tunnels that introduce fragmentation, should be particularly cautious.
sections.plainLanguage: You can avoid cutting messages into pieces, or put a stronger lock on each message so wrongly glued ones are thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who knows two hosts are using a fragmented stream can corrupt it by sending forged-source fragments with an offset greater than zero. This needs only the source and destination addresses, the protocol number and the fragment boundaries, not port or sequence numbers.

If the attacker can see packets on the path, the attack resembles injecting full segments. It makes blind disruption easier and might be used to degrade service. The authors believe only streams using IPv4 fragmentation are likely vulnerable, and that IPv4 fragmentation may not be advisable for critical applications regardless of security concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone sneaky who knows who is talking can slip in fake pieces so the real message gets ruined.
